Code 
library(tidyverse)

orders <- read_csv("data/orders.csv")
order_items <- read_csv("data/order_items.csv")
products <- read_csv("data/products.csv")
sellers <- read_csv("data/sellers.csv")

orders_clean <- orders |>
  filter(order_status == "delivered") |>
  filter(!is.na(delivery_days)) |>
  mutate(
    delivery_status = if_else(
      delivery_days <= estimated_days,
      "On Time",
      "Late"
    )
  )

supply_chain_data <- orders_clean |>
  left_join(order_items, by = "order_id") |>
  left_join(sellers, by = "seller_id") |>
  left_join(products, by = "product_id") |>
  mutate(
    freight_ratio = freight_value / price
  )

This exploration looks at how seller scale, delivery performance, freight cost, and product characteristics interact across the marketplace.

The goal is not only to identify expensive or delayed shipments, but to understand where marketplace growth is efficient and where operational attention could have the largest impact.

Business question: Which seller segments are helping the marketplace scale efficiently, and which ones are creating high fulfillment costs or weak operational performance?

Marketplace benchmark

Before comparing seller groups, I first calculated overall marketplace performance.

Code 
overall_performance <- supply_chain_data |>
  summarise(
    total_items = n(),
    average_delivery_days = mean(delivery_days),
    average_freight_cost = mean(freight_value),
    average_freight_ratio = mean(freight_ratio, na.rm = TRUE),
    on_time_rate = mean(delivery_status == "On Time") * 100
  )

overall_performance
# A tibble: 1 × 5
  total_items average_delivery_days average_freight_cost average_freight_ratio
        <int>                 <dbl>                <dbl>                 <dbl>
1      110189                  12.0                 20.0                 0.321
# ℹ 1 more variable: on_time_rate <dbl>

The marketplace contains 110189 item rows.

Average delivery time is 12 days, average freight cost is 20, and the overall on-time delivery rate is 92.6%.

These values provide the benchmark for the rest of the analysis.

Code 
state_names <- tibble(
  seller_state = c(
    "SP", "MG", "PR", "RJ",
    "SC", "RS", "DF", "BA"
  ),
  seller_name = c(
    "São Paulo",
    "Minas Gerais",
    "Paraná",
    "Rio de Janeiro",
    "Santa Catarina",
    "Rio Grande do Sul",
    "Federal District",
    "Bahia"
  )
)

seller_state_performance <- supply_chain_data |>
  group_by(seller_state) |>
  summarise(
    total_items = n(),
    average_delivery_days = mean(delivery_days),
    average_freight_cost = mean(freight_value),
    average_freight_ratio = mean(freight_ratio, na.rm = TRUE),
    on_time_rate = mean(delivery_status == "On Time") * 100,
    average_product_weight = mean(product_weight_g, na.rm = TRUE)
  ) |>
  arrange(desc(total_items)) |>
  left_join(state_names, by = "seller_state")

top_8_states <- seller_state_performance |>
  head(8)

largest_state <- top_8_states |>
  arrange(desc(total_items)) |>
  head(1)

largest_state_share <-
  largest_state$total_items /
  overall_performance$total_items * 100

1. Where scale meets reliability

The first question is whether the seller groups handling the most marketplace activity are also delivering reliably.

1a. Volume and delivery performance

This chart combines marketplace volume, on-time delivery performance, and average freight cost.

Code 
ggplot(
  top_8_states,
  aes(
    x = total_items,
    y = on_time_rate,
    size = average_freight_cost,
    color = seller_name
  )
) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.85) +
  geom_hline(
    yintercept = overall_performance$on_time_rate,
    linetype = "dashed",
    color = "#555555"
  ) +
  labs(
    title = "Scale does not always guarantee stronger fulfillment",
    subtitle = "Bubble size represents average freight cost",
    x = "Number of Items",
    y = "On-Time Delivery Rate (%)",
    color = "Seller State",
    size = "Average Freight Cost"
  ) +
  theme_light()

What this shows: São Paulo handles 78598 items, representing about 71.3% of marketplace activity.

Because of its scale, even a relatively small operational change in this seller group could affect a large number of marketplace items.

1b. Above or below the benchmark

The next chart compares each major seller state’s on-time delivery performance directly with the marketplace average.

Code 
delivery_comparison <- top_8_states |>
  mutate(
    difference_from_average =
      on_time_rate - overall_performance$on_time_rate
  )

best_delivery_state <- delivery_comparison |>
  arrange(desc(difference_from_average)) |>
  head(1)

weakest_delivery_state <- delivery_comparison |>
  arrange(difference_from_average) |>
  head(1)
Code 
ggplot(
  delivery_comparison,
  aes(
    x = difference_from_average,
    y = reorder(seller_name, difference_from_average)
  )
) +
  geom_vline(
    xintercept = 0,
    linetype = "dashed",
    color = "#555555"
  ) +
  geom_segment(
    aes(
      x = 0,
      xend = difference_from_average,
      y = reorder(seller_name, difference_from_average),
      yend = reorder(seller_name, difference_from_average)
    ),
    linewidth = 1,
    color = "#6C757D"
  ) +
  geom_point(
    aes(color = difference_from_average > 0),
    size = 4
  ) +
  scale_color_manual(
    values = c(
      "TRUE" = "#2A9D8F",
      "FALSE" = "#E63946"
    ),
    labels = c(
      "FALSE" = "Below Average",
      "TRUE" = "Above Average"
    )
  ) +
  labs(
    title = "Major seller states fall on both sides of the delivery benchmark",
    subtitle = "Distance from the overall marketplace on-time rate",
    x = "Percentage Points Above or Below Marketplace Average",
    y = "Seller State",
    color = "Performance"
  ) +
  theme_light()

What this shows: Rio Grande do Sul performs strongest relative to the marketplace benchmark, while São Paulo has the weakest performance among the eight largest seller states.

This matters because weak performance becomes more important when it occurs in a seller group handling substantial marketplace volume.

2. Where operations start to slip

Delivery performance and freight burden should not be evaluated separately.

A seller group with strong delivery and low freight burden occupies a very different operating position from one with weaker delivery and higher freight cost relative to product price.

Code 
ggplot(
  top_8_states,
  aes(
    x = average_freight_ratio,
    y = on_time_rate,
    size = total_items,
    color = seller_name
  )
) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.85) +
  geom_vline(
    xintercept = overall_performance$average_freight_ratio,
    linetype = "dashed",
    color = "#555555"
  ) +
  geom_hline(
    yintercept = overall_performance$on_time_rate,
    linetype = "dashed",
    color = "#555555"
  ) +
  labs(
    title = "Seller states occupy very different operating positions",
    subtitle = "Bubble size represents marketplace item volume",
    x = "Average Freight-to-Price Ratio",
    y = "On-Time Delivery Rate (%)",
    color = "Seller State",
    size = "Number of Items"
  ) +
  theme_light()

What this shows: Seller groups above the horizontal benchmark have stronger-than-average delivery performance.

Seller groups to the right of the vertical benchmark have a higher-than-average freight burden.

The groups that combine weaker delivery with higher freight burden deserve the closest operational attention, especially when their bubbles are large.

3. When does marketplace pressure peak?

Seller performance should also be viewed through time.

A seller network may operate differently during low-volume and high-volume periods, so I summarized marketplace activity by month and year.

Code 
monthly_activity <- supply_chain_data |>
  group_by(purchase_year, purchase_month) |>
  summarise(
    total_items = n(),
    on_time_rate = mean(delivery_status == "On Time") * 100
  )
`summarise()` has regrouped the output.
ℹ Summaries were computed grouped by purchase_year and purchase_month.
ℹ Output is grouped by purchase_year.
ℹ Use `summarise(.groups = "drop_last")` to silence this message.
ℹ Use `summarise(.by = c(purchase_year, purchase_month))` for per-operation
  grouping (`?dplyr::dplyr_by`) instead.
Code 
peak_month <- monthly_activity |>
  arrange(desc(total_items)) |>
  head(1)

Area + line + points

The area emphasizes the amount of marketplace activity.

The line shows the direction of change, while the points make individual months easier to identify.

Code 
ggplot(
  monthly_activity,
  aes(
    x = purchase_month,
    y = total_items,
    group = 1
  )
) +
  geom_area(
    fill = "#4CC9F0",
    alpha = 0.45
  ) +
  geom_line(
    color = "#3A0CA3",
    linewidth = 1.3
  ) +
  geom_point(
    color = "#F72585",
    size = 3
  ) +
  facet_wrap(~ purchase_year) +
  labs(
    title = "Marketplace pressure changes sharply across the year",
    subtitle = "Area shows volume while the line and points highlight the monthly pattern",
    x = "Purchase Month",
    y = "Number of Items"
  ) +
  theme_light()

What this shows: The highest-volume period occurs in month 11 of 2017, with 8474 items.

The on-time delivery rate during that period was approximately 87.1%.

This helps management identify when the marketplace is experiencing its greatest fulfillment workload.

4. Cost or product mix?

Higher freight cost does not automatically mean that a seller is operating inefficiently.

Product characteristics may explain part of the freight burden.

4a. Does weight explain freight cost?

Code 
supply_chain_data |>
  filter(!is.na(product_weight_g)) |>
  ggplot(
    aes(
      x = product_weight_g,
      y = freight_value
    )
  ) +
  geom_point(
    color = "#4361EE",
    alpha = 0.12
  ) +
  geom_smooth(
    color = "#F72585",
    se = FALSE,
    linewidth = 1.4
  ) +
  labs(
    title = "Heavier products generally cost more to ship",
    subtitle = "The highlighted trend shows the overall relationship",
    x = "Product Weight (grams)",
    y = "Freight Cost"
  ) +
  theme_light()

What this shows: Freight cost generally rises as product weight increases.

This means higher freight cost should not automatically be treated as evidence of weak seller performance.

Product mix explains at least part of the logistics difference.

4b. Does the pattern change by seller state?

The next chart takes the overall relationship from 4.a and separates it across the four largest seller states.

The observations are kept light so the state-specific trend lines become the main focus.

Code 
top_4_states <- top_8_states |>
  head(4)

top_4_state_names <- top_4_states$seller_name
Code 
supply_chain_data |>
  left_join(state_names, by = "seller_state") |>
  filter(seller_name %in% top_4_state_names) |>
  filter(!is.na(product_weight_g)) |>
  ggplot(
    aes(
      x = product_weight_g,
      y = freight_value
    )
  ) +
  geom_point(
    color = "gray60",
    alpha = 0.12
  ) +
  geom_smooth(
    aes(color = seller_name),
    se = FALSE,
    linewidth = 1.4
  ) +
  facet_wrap(~ seller_name) +
  scale_color_manual(
    values = c(
      "São Paulo" = "#F72585",
      "Minas Gerais" = "#4361EE",
      "Paraná" = "#F8961E",
      "Rio de Janeiro" = "#2A9D8F"
    )
  ) +
  labs(
    title = "Product weight matters, but the freight pattern changes by state",
    subtitle = "Each colored trend highlights the weight–freight relationship within a major seller state",
    x = "Product Weight (grams)",
    y = "Freight Cost",
    color = "Seller State"
  ) +
  guides(
    color = "none"
  ) +
  theme_light()

What this shows: All four major seller states show a positive relationship between product weight and freight cost, but the strength and shape of that relationship are not identical.

The colored lines make these differences easier to compare.

This suggests that product weight explains part of the freight burden, while seller location and other fulfillment factors may still contribute.

5. Are averages hiding risk?

Average freight cost can hide important differences in the underlying shipment distribution.

For this reason, the next chart combines two geoms:

  • violin plot → shows the overall distribution,
  • boxplot → highlights the center and spread.
Code 
top_5_states <- top_8_states |>
  head(5)

top_5_state_names <- top_5_states$seller_name

highest_freight_state <- top_5_states |>
  arrange(desc(average_freight_cost)) |>
  head(1)
Code 
supply_chain_data |>
  left_join(state_names, by = "seller_state") |>
  filter(seller_name %in% top_5_state_names) |>
  ggplot(
    aes(
      x = seller_name,
      y = freight_value,
      fill = seller_name,
      color = seller_name
    )
  ) +
  geom_violin(
    alpha = 0.45
  ) +
  geom_boxplot(
    width = 0.14,
    alpha = 0.75
  ) +
  scale_fill_manual(
    values = c(
      "São Paulo" = "#F72585",
      "Minas Gerais" = "#4361EE",
      "Paraná" = "#F8961E",
      "Rio de Janeiro" = "#2A9D8F",
      "Santa Catarina" = "#9B5DE5"
    )
  ) +
  scale_color_manual(
    values = c(
      "São Paulo" = "#F72585",
      "Minas Gerais" = "#4361EE",
      "Paraná" = "#F8961E",
      "Rio de Janeiro" = "#2A9D8F",
      "Santa Catarina" = "#9B5DE5"
    )
  ) +
  labs(
    title = "Average freight cost hides very different shipment patterns",
    subtitle = "Violin shows the distribution while the boxplot highlights center and spread",
    x = "Seller State",
    y = "Freight Cost",
    fill = "Seller State",
    color = "Seller State"
  ) +
  guides(
    fill = "none",
    color = "none"
  ) +
  theme_light()

What this shows: Santa Catarina has the highest average freight cost among the five largest seller states, at approximately 26.

The distribution shows something that averages cannot.

Some seller states have a much wider freight-cost spread, meaning management may be dealing with occasional very expensive shipments rather than consistently high cost across every order.

6. What should management do next?

The exploration shows that seller performance should not be judged using volume, delivery performance, or freight cost alone.

The strongest seller groups are those that combine meaningful marketplace scale with reliable delivery and a reasonable freight burden.

Management should pay particular attention to seller groups that combine:

  • high marketplace volume,
  • delivery performance below the marketplace benchmark,
  • freight burden above the marketplace benchmark,
  • unusually wide freight-cost variation, and
  • freight costs that cannot be fully explained by heavier products.

The time analysis also identifies when marketplace workload reaches its highest levels.

Together, these findings help separate scalable seller performance from areas where targeted operational improvement could have the largest marketplace impact.

```{r}
library(tidyverse)

orders <- read_csv("data/orders.csv")
order_items <- read_csv("data/order_items.csv")

sellers <- read_csv("data/sellers.csv")

orders_clean <- orders |>
  filter(order_status == "delivered") |>
  filter(!is.na(delivery_days)) |>
  mutate(

      delivery_days <= estimated_days,

    )
  )

supply_chain_data <- orders_clean |>
  left_join(order_items, by = "order_id") |>
  left_join(sellers, by = "seller_id") |>
  left_join(products, by = "product_id") |>

```

This exploration looks at how seller scale, delivery performance, freight cost, and product characteristics interact across the marketplace.

The goal is not only to identify expensive or delayed shipments, but to understand where marketplace growth is efficient and where operational attention could have the largest impact.

**Business question:** Which seller segments are helping the marketplace scale efficiently, and which ones are creating high fulfillment costs or weak operational performance?

## Marketplace benchmark

Before comparing seller groups, I first calculated overall marketplace performance.

```{r}
overall_performance <- supply_chain_data |>
  summarise(
    total_items = n(),
    average_delivery_days = mean(delivery_days),
    average_freight_cost = mean(freight_value),
    average_freight_ratio = mean(freight_ratio, na.rm = TRUE),
    on_time_rate = mean(delivery_status == "On Time") * 100
  )

overall_performance
```

The marketplace contains **`r overall_performance$total_items` item rows**.

Average delivery time is **`r round(overall_performance$average_delivery_days, 1)` days**, average freight cost is **`r round(overall_performance$average_freight_cost, 1)`**, and the overall on-time delivery rate is **`r round(overall_performance$on_time_rate, 1)`%**.

These values provide the benchmark for the rest of the analysis.

```{r}
state_names <- tibble(
  seller_state = c(
    "SP", "MG", "PR", "RJ",
    "SC", "RS", "DF", "BA"
  ),
  seller_name = c(
    "São Paulo",
    "Minas Gerais",
    "Paraná",
    "Rio de Janeiro",
    "Santa Catarina",
    "Rio Grande do Sul",
    "Federal District",
    "Bahia"
  )
)

seller_state_performance <- supply_chain_data |>
  group_by(seller_state) |>
  summarise(
    total_items = n(),
    average_delivery_days = mean(delivery_days),
    average_freight_cost = mean(freight_value),
    average_freight_ratio = mean(freight_ratio, na.rm = TRUE),
    on_time_rate = mean(delivery_status == "On Time") * 100,
    average_product_weight = mean(product_weight_g, na.rm = TRUE)
  ) |>
  arrange(desc(total_items)) |>
  left_join(state_names, by = "seller_state")

top_8_states <- seller_state_performance |>
  head(8)

largest_state <- top_8_states |>
  arrange(desc(total_items)) |>
  head(1)

largest_state_share <-
  largest_state$total_items /
  overall_performance$total_items * 100
```

## 1. Where scale meets reliability

The first question is whether the seller groups handling the most marketplace activity are also delivering reliably.

### 1a. Volume and delivery performance

This chart combines marketplace volume, on-time delivery performance, and average freight cost.

```{r}
ggplot(
  top_8_states,
  aes(
    x = total_items,
    y = on_time_rate,
    size = average_freight_cost,
    color = seller_name
  )
) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.85) +
  geom_hline(
    yintercept = overall_performance$on_time_rate,
    linetype = "dashed",
    color = "#555555"
  ) +
  labs(
    title = "Scale does not always guarantee stronger fulfillment",
    subtitle = "Bubble size represents average freight cost",
    x = "Number of Items",
    y = "On-Time Delivery Rate (%)",
    color = "Seller State",
    size = "Average Freight Cost"
  ) +
  theme_light()
```

**What this shows:** **`r largest_state$seller_name`** handles **`r largest_state$total_items` items**, representing about **`r round(largest_state_share, 1)`%** of marketplace activity.

Because of its scale, even a relatively small operational change in this seller group could affect a large number of marketplace items.

### 1b. Above or below the benchmark

The next chart compares each major seller state's on-time delivery performance directly with the marketplace average.

```{r}
delivery_comparison <- top_8_states |>
  mutate(
    difference_from_average =
      on_time_rate - overall_performance$on_time_rate
  )

best_delivery_state <- delivery_comparison |>
  arrange(desc(difference_from_average)) |>
  head(1)

weakest_delivery_state <- delivery_comparison |>
  arrange(difference_from_average) |>
  head(1)
```

```{r}
ggplot(
  delivery_comparison,
  aes(
    x = difference_from_average,
    y = reorder(seller_name, difference_from_average)
  )
) +
  geom_vline(
    xintercept = 0,
    linetype = "dashed",
    color = "#555555"
  ) +
  geom_segment(
    aes(
      x = 0,
      xend = difference_from_average,
      y = reorder(seller_name, difference_from_average),
      yend = reorder(seller_name, difference_from_average)
    ),
    linewidth = 1,
    color = "#6C757D"
  ) +
  geom_point(
    aes(color = difference_from_average > 0),
    size = 4
  ) +
  scale_color_manual(
    values = c(
      "TRUE" = "#2A9D8F",
      "FALSE" = "#E63946"
    ),
    labels = c(
      "FALSE" = "Below Average",
      "TRUE" = "Above Average"
    )
  ) +
  labs(
    title = "Major seller states fall on both sides of the delivery benchmark",
    subtitle = "Distance from the overall marketplace on-time rate",
    x = "Percentage Points Above or Below Marketplace Average",
    y = "Seller State",
    color = "Performance"
  ) +
  theme_light()
```

**What this shows:** **`r best_delivery_state$seller_name`** performs strongest relative to the marketplace benchmark, while **`r weakest_delivery_state$seller_name`** has the weakest performance among the eight largest seller states.

This matters because weak performance becomes more important when it occurs in a seller group handling substantial marketplace volume.

A seller group with strong delivery and low freight burden occupies a very different operating position from one with weaker delivery and higher freight cost relative to product price.

**What this shows:** Seller groups above the horizontal benchmark have stronger-than-average delivery performance.

Seller groups to the right of the vertical benchmark have a higher-than-average freight burden.

The groups that combine weaker delivery with higher freight burden deserve the closest operational attention, especially when their bubbles are large.

## 3. When does marketplace pressure peak?

Seller performance should also be viewed through time.

A seller network may operate differently during low-volume and high-volume periods, so I summarized marketplace activity by month and year.

### Area + line + points

The area emphasizes the amount of marketplace activity.

This helps management identify when the marketplace is experiencing its greatest fulfillment workload.

```{r}
  ) +
  labs(
    title = "Heavier products generally cost more to ship",
    subtitle = "The highlighted trend shows the overall relationship",
    x = "Product Weight (grams)",
    y = "Freight Cost"
  ) +
  theme_light()
```

**What this shows:** Freight cost generally rises as product weight increases.

This means higher freight cost should not automatically be treated as evidence of weak seller performance.

Product mix explains at least part of the logistics difference.

### 4b. Does the pattern change by seller state?

The next chart takes the overall relationship from 4.a and separates it across the four largest seller states.

The observations are kept light so the state-specific trend lines become the main focus.

```{r}
top_4_states <- top_8_states |>
  head(4)

top_4_state_names <- top_4_states$seller_name
```

```{r}
#| message: false
#| warning: false

supply_chain_data |>
  left_join(state_names, by = "seller_state") |>
  filter(seller_name %in% top_4_state_names) |>
  filter(!is.na(product_weight_g)) |>
  ggplot(
    aes(
      x = product_weight_g,
      y = freight_value
    )
  ) +
  geom_point(
    color = "gray60",
    alpha = 0.12
  ) +
  geom_smooth(
    aes(color = seller_name),
    se = FALSE,
    linewidth = 1.4
  ) +
  facet_wrap(~ seller_name) +
  scale_color_manual(
    values = c(
      "São Paulo" = "#F72585",
      "Minas Gerais" = "#4361EE",
      "Paraná" = "#F8961E",
      "Rio de Janeiro" = "#2A9D8F"
    )
  ) +
  labs(
    title = "Product weight matters, but the freight pattern changes by state",
    subtitle = "Each colored trend highlights the weight–freight relationship within a major seller state",
    x = "Product Weight (grams)",
    y = "Freight Cost",
    color = "Seller State"
  ) +
  guides(
    color = "none"
  ) +
  theme_light()
```

**What this shows:** All four major seller states show a positive relationship between product weight and freight cost, but the strength and shape of that relationship are not identical.

The colored lines make these differences easier to compare.

This suggests that product weight explains part of the freight burden, while seller location and other fulfillment factors may still contribute.

## 5. Are averages hiding risk?

Average freight cost can hide important differences in the underlying shipment distribution.

For this reason, the next chart combines two geoms:

- violin plot → shows the overall distribution,
- boxplot → highlights the center and spread.

```{r}
top_5_states <- top_8_states |>
  head(5)

top_5_state_names <- top_5_states$seller_name

highest_freight_state <- top_5_states |>
  arrange(desc(average_freight_cost)) |>
  head(1)
```

```{r}
supply_chain_data |>
  left_join(state_names, by = "seller_state") |>
  filter(seller_name %in% top_5_state_names) |>
  ggplot(
    aes(
      x = seller_name,
      y = freight_value,
      fill = seller_name,
      color = seller_name
    )
  ) +
  geom_violin(
    alpha = 0.45
  ) +
  geom_boxplot(
    width = 0.14,
    alpha = 0.75
  ) +
  scale_fill_manual(
    values = c(
      "São Paulo" = "#F72585",
      "Minas Gerais" = "#4361EE",
      "Paraná" = "#F8961E",
      "Rio de Janeiro" = "#2A9D8F",
      "Santa Catarina" = "#9B5DE5"
    )
  ) +
  scale_color_manual(
    values = c(
      "São Paulo" = "#F72585",
      "Minas Gerais" = "#4361EE",
      "Paraná" = "#F8961E",
      "Rio de Janeiro" = "#2A9D8F",
      "Santa Catarina" = "#9B5DE5"
    )
  ) +
  labs(
    title = "Average freight cost hides very different shipment patterns",
    subtitle = "Violin shows the distribution while the boxplot highlights center and spread",
    x = "Seller State",
    y = "Freight Cost",
    fill = "Seller State",
    color = "Seller State"
  ) +
  guides(
    fill = "none",
    color = "none"
  ) +
  theme_light()
```

**What this shows:** **`r highest_freight_state$seller_name`** has the highest average freight cost among the five largest seller states, at approximately **`r round(highest_freight_state$average_freight_cost, 1)`**.

The distribution shows something that averages cannot.

Some seller states have a much wider freight-cost spread, meaning management may be dealing with occasional very expensive shipments rather than consistently high cost across every order.

## 6. What should management do next?

The exploration shows that seller performance should not be judged using volume, delivery performance, or freight cost alone.

The strongest seller groups are those that combine meaningful marketplace scale with reliable delivery and a reasonable freight burden.

Management should pay particular attention to seller groups that combine:

- high marketplace volume,
- delivery performance below the marketplace benchmark,
- freight burden above the marketplace benchmark,
- unusually wide freight-cost variation, and
- freight costs that cannot be fully explained by heavier products.

The time analysis also identifies when marketplace workload reaches its highest levels.

Together, these findings help separate scalable seller performance from areas where targeted operational improvement could have the largest marketplace impact.
